Clear
klēr
adj. and v. (bright, transparent; free of guilt; to acquit; rendering Hebrew naqah, zakah, and bar, Greek hagnos)
Latin clarus, bright, through Old French cler. The moral sense — clear of a charge — grows from the physical one: nothing in the way of the light.

Biblical Definition

The Name proclaimed to Moses ends with the word: the LORD is “forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty” (Exo 34:7). Judah, caught with the cup, asks, “how shall we clear ourselves? God hath found out the iniquity of thy servants” (Gen 44:16). David confesses so that God may “be clear when thou judgest” (Psa 51:4). Paul's Corinthians, having repented, “approved yourselves to be clear in this matter” (2Co 7:11). The bride is “clear as the sun” (Sng 6:10), the light of the city is “clear as crystal” (Rev 21:11), and the river of life proceeds from the throne “clear as crystal” (Rev 22:1). A servant released from an oath is “clear from this my oath” (Gen 24:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines clear as free from darkness or obscurity; transparent; free from guilt or blame; innocent; and, as a verb, to free from guilt, to acquit.

expand to see more

CLEAR, a. Open; free from obstruction; free from clouds or darkness; bright; transparent.

2. Free from guilt or blame; innocent; unspotted; irreproachable.

3. Free from any thing that may be an impediment; free from debt or obligation.

CLEAR, v.t. To free from guilt or the imputation of guilt; to acquit; to justify.

Key Scripture

Exo 34:7 — "Keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty; visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, and upon the children's children, unto the third and to the fourth generation."

Psa 51:4 — "Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight: that thou mightest be justified when thou speakest, and be clear when thou judgest."

Gen 44:16 — "And Judah said, What shall we say unto my lord? what shall we speak? or how shall we clear ourselves? God hath found out the iniquity of thy servants: behold, we are my lord's servants, both we, and he also with whom the cup is found."

Rev 22:1 — "And he shewed me a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb."

2Co 7:11 — "For behold this selfsame thing, that ye sorrowed after a godly sort, what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear, yea, what vehement desire, yea, what zeal, yea, what revenge! In all things ye have approved yourselves to be clear in this matter."

Sng 6:10 — "Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners?"

Modern Corruption

The Name is quoted as far as forgiving iniquity and cut off before by no means clearing the guilty.

expand to see more

Exodus 34:6–7 is the fullest self-description God gives in the Old Testament, and modern religion recites the first half of it. Merciful, gracious, longsuffering, abundant in goodness and truth, forgiving iniquity — and then the clause that is dropped: “that will by no means clear the guilty.” Both halves are the gospel. God forgives, and God does not acquit the guilty, and the cross is the one place where both are true of the same sinner at the same moment: “that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus” (Rom 3:26). Justification is not God clearing the guilty. It is God counting righteous those whose guilt has already been borne by Another.

Genesis 44:16 is the turn of the Joseph story. For twenty-two years the brothers have been clearing themselves; when the cup is found in Benjamin's sack Judah stops: “how shall we clear ourselves? God hath found out the iniquity of thy servants.” He is not speaking of the cup. Reconciliation begins where self-justification ends. David goes one step further in Psalm 51:4 and clears God instead of himself — “that thou mightest be justified when thou speakest, and be clear when thou judgest” — which Paul quotes in Romans 3:4 as the posture of every true confession: let God be true, and every man a liar.

Second Corinthians 7:11 shows what a cleared conscience looks like from the outside. Godly sorrow wrought carefulness, clearing of themselves, indignation, fear, vehement desire, zeal, revenge — and by these the Corinthians “approved yourselves to be clear.” They were cleared by dealing with the matter, not by denying it. Cheap grace clears by forgetting; the apostolic church cleared by repenting.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew naqah (H5352), to be clean, acquitted, held innocent; zakah (H2135), to be pure, clear; tsadaq (H6663), to be just, to justify oneself; bar (H1249), pure, clear; Greek hagnos (G53), pure; krystallizo (G2929), to shine like crystal.

expand to see more

Hebrew naqah (H5352) — to be clean, acquitted, left unpunished; Exodus 34:7, Numbers 14:18, Genesis 24:8, Nahum 1:3.

Hebrew zakah (H2135) — to be clear, pure, justified; Psalm 51:4, Job 15:14, 25:4.

Hebrew tsadaq (H6663) — to be righteous, to justify oneself; Genesis 44:16, “how shall we clear ourselves?”

Greek hagnos (G53) — pure, clear; 2 Corinthians 7:11; and krystallizo (G2929), clear as crystal, Revelation 21:11.

Usage

"“Will by no means clear the guilty” — the half of the Name men forget."

"“How shall we clear ourselves?” — the end of self-justification, and the beginning of reconciliation."

"“Clear as crystal” — the river from the throne."
